scenes.title: Refresh OLS, 2SLS and projection matrices
scenes.objective: Recover the estimators that appear as k-class special cases.
body: The k-class family connects several estimators used in simultaneous-equation models. OLS and 2SLS appear at particular values of a scalar parameter κ.
To understand the family, recall the instrument projection P_Z and its residual-maker complement M_Z.

items.recall: The projection matrix onto the column space of the instrument matrix Z.
refresh: It is symmetric and idempotent, so it projects vectors onto the instrument space.
The fitted component is P_Z times the vector being projected.
M_Z removes the component explained by the instrument space.
It is also symmetric and idempotent when P_Z is a projection matrix.
The identity I−M_Z=P_Z is the key step in showing that κ=1 gives 2SLS.
2SLS projects the structural regressors through the instrument space.
The projected cross-products replace the ordinary OLS cross-products.
The k-class formula contains this expression at κ=1.

ask.q: What identity connects the projection and residual-maker matrices?
ask.nudge: The projection plus its residual-maker equals the identity matrix.

scenes.title: One estimator family, different values of κ
scenes.objective: Build an intuitive picture of the k-class continuum.
body: The k-class estimator changes how much of the instrument-residual component is removed from the cross-products. At κ=0, nothing is removed and the estimator is OLS. At κ=1, the full instrument projection remains and the estimator is 2SLS.
Other values of κ generate other members of the family. LIML chooses a value using a likelihood/eigenvalue criterion rather than setting κ mechanically to zero or one.

scenario.title: Check the two special cases
body: An analyst has a structural regressor matrix X and an instrument projection P_Z. Define M_Z=I−P_Z and consider the k-class estimator.
At κ=0, the factor I−κM_Z equals I, so the formula reduces to (X′X)⁻¹X′Y, the OLS estimator.
At κ=1, the factor becomes I−M_Z=P_Z, so the estimator is (X′P_ZX)⁻¹X′P_ZY, the 2SLS estimator.
These endpoint checks are the fastest way to verify whether a proposed k-class formula has been written correctly.
scenario.q: Which estimator is obtained at κ=1?

ask.q: What is the estimator at κ=0?

scenes.title: The general k-class formula
scenes.objective: Write and interpret the estimator using M_Z.

blocks.body: β̂(κ)=[X′(I−κM_Z)X]⁻¹X′(I−κM_Z)Y, where M_Z=I−P_Z and P_Z is the projection onto the instrument space.
At κ=0, I−κM_Z=I. The estimator becomes (X′X)⁻¹X′Y, the ordinary least-squares estimator.
At κ=1, I−M_Z=P_Z. The estimator becomes (X′P_ZX)⁻¹X′P_ZY, the two-stage least-squares estimator.
The parameter κ indexes the estimator within the k-class family. It is not the number of regressors, the number of instruments or the number of restrictions.

scenes.title: LIML and the Fuller adjustment
scenes.objective: Explain how LIML and Fuller fit into the k-class family.

blocks.body: LIML is a k-class estimator whose κ is selected from a likelihood or generalized eigenvalue criterion associated with the structural equation and instrument set.

In some finite-sample settings, especially with many or weak instruments, LIML can have more favourable median-bias behaviour than 2SLS. It still depends on valid instruments and adequate identification.
Fuller estimation adjusts the LIML parameter to improve finite-sample behaviour. The adjustment depends on a chosen constant and sample degrees of freedom.
Neither LIML nor Fuller makes an instrument relevant or restores exclusion. Weak-identification-robust inference and a credible instrument design remain important.

ask.q: What does LIML choose within the k-class family?
ask.nudge: It selects the value of the k-class parameter κ.

scenes.title: Why estimator choice does not replace instrument validity
scenes.objective: Separate finite-sample estimator properties from identification assumptions.
body: OLS, 2SLS and LIML differ in how they use the regressor and instrument information. But an IV-based estimator still needs instruments that predict endogenous regressors and satisfy exclusion.
A different κ may improve finite-sample behaviour in some settings, but it cannot remove a direct instrument-to-outcome path or create strong first-stage variation.

scenario.teaser: Many weak instruments in a small sample
scenario.title: LIML is not a magic fix
body: A researcher has many excluded instruments relative to the sample size. The first stages are weak, and 2SLS estimates are highly variable.
LIML may have more favourable finite-sample median bias in some such designs, and a Fuller adjustment may further improve finite-sample behaviour.
However, if an instrument directly affects the outcome or is correlated with the structural disturbance, LIML remains inconsistent. If the instruments are weak, inference can still be unreliable.
The estimator choice should be accompanied by first-stage diagnostics, weak-instrument-robust inference and a substantive exclusion argument.
scenario.q: What problem can LIML not solve?
scenario.answer: It cannot repair invalid exclusion or eliminate weak identification.

ask.q: What is the key distinction between LIML's finite-sample property and instrument validity?
ask.nudge: One concerns estimator behaviour; the other concerns identifying assumptions.

items.claim: The k-class parameter κ is the number of regressors.

items.why: The matrix factor becomes the identity.

scenes.title: Transfer problem: compute an intermediate k-class value
scenes.objective: Calculate a k-class estimate from cross-products.
scenes.problem: Use X′X=10, X′M_ZX=4, X′Y=20 and X′M_ZY=5. Calculate β̂(0.5) and explain how it lies between the OLS and 2SLS endpoint values in this example.
hints: Write the scalar numerator and denominator.
Compare the result with κ=0 and κ=1.
scenes.answer: β̂(0.5)=(20−2.5)/(10−2)=17.5/8=2.1875; it lies between OLS 2 and 2SLS 2.5 in this example.

ask.q: Does an intermediate κ always produce a coefficient between OLS and 2SLS?
ask.nudge: This is true for the supplied scalar example, not a universal monotonicity theorem.

scenes.title: Summary: the k-class family
scenes.objective: Compress the estimator relationships into an exam-ready checklist.
body: The k-class estimator is β̂(κ)=[X′(I−κM_Z)X]⁻¹X′(I−κM_Z)Y, where M_Z=I−P_Z. At κ=0 it becomes OLS; at κ=1 it becomes 2SLS.

LIML chooses κ through a likelihood or generalized eigenvalue criterion. Fuller estimation adjusts LIML for finite-sample behaviour. In some many/weak-instrument settings, LIML may have more favourable median bias than 2SLS.
All IV-based estimators still require relevant and valid instruments. Neither LIML nor Fuller repairs exclusion failure or removes weak-identification concerns.

ask.q: What are the two endpoint checks for a k-class formula?
ask.nudge: Set κ to zero and one.

scenes.title: Extension — scalar k-class algebra
scenes.objective: Derive the scalar cross-product expression used in calculations.

blocks.body: For one coefficient, β̂(κ)=(X′Y−κX′M_ZY)/(X′X−κX′M_ZX). This is obtained by expanding the general matrix formula.
At κ=0, β̂=X′Y/X′X. At κ=1, subtract the residual-maker cross-products, leaving the projected instrument-space cross-products.
The denominator must be nonzero for the scalar estimator to exist. In the matrix case, X′(I−κM_Z)X must be nonsingular.
